lesson.title: No One in Charge: The Peer-to-Peer Model
lesson.summary: The peer-to-peer model discards the client-server split entirely: every participating host can act as both provider and consumer, and there is no single, centralized party the whole system depends on.
lesson.body:
Where the client-server model assigns two fixed, asymmetric roles, the peer-to-peer model treats every participating host as functionally equivalent. There is no party that is always the one waiting for connections and never initiates them, and no party that is always the one initiating and never accepts them. Any peer can connect out to another peer, and any peer can accept an incoming connection from another peer, and the same host is regularly acting as what would be called a server for one exchange and a client for another, sometimes simultaneously. This symmetry is the defining trait of the model, roles are interchangeable rather than fixed.

The practical consequence is decentralization. In a client-server system, data and control live at the server. In a peer-to-peer system, they are spread across the participating hosts themselves, with no single host that the whole system depends on to keep functioning. If one peer goes offline, the system does not necessarily stop working, other peers can often still reach each other and continue, whereas losing the server in a client-server system takes down access for every client at once. This is part of why peer-to-peer designs show up in file-sharing systems, some messaging and video-call systems, and blockchain networks, the workload and the responsibility for staying available get distributed across many participants instead of concentrated in one place that its operators have to keep running and scaled up.

The tradeoff is that a peer-to-peer system gives up the easy consistency and central authority the client-server model provides for free. With no single party holding an authoritative copy of anything, peers that want to agree on shared state have to actively coordinate with each other to reach that agreement, which is a genuinely harder problem than a server simply deciding. Peer-to-peer systems also tend to need their own way of finding other peers in the first place, some kind of discovery mechanism, sometimes centralized ironically enough and sometimes not, since there is no fixed, well-known address to connect to the way there is for a server.

There is a further practical wrinkle that is specific to peer-to-peer networking on the real internet. Because any host, not just designated servers, needs to be reachable by other hosts to accept an incoming connection, and most hosts today sit behind a NAT device, a home router, for instance, that does not allow arbitrary unsolicited inbound connections, peers frequently cannot simply connect to each other the way a client connects to a well-known server. Working around that limitation is its own problem, NAT traversal, covered next.
